full_text:
Interviewer:	OK, when did you start your placement?

Subject:	Um, June, I think.

Interviewer:	Until June next year?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, it’s a year, one year.

Interviewer:	OK, can you tell me a bit about [company] and what they do?

Subject:	Right, um, we’re not allowed to tell you loads because of our confidentiality thing, but (That’s ok) basically they just do um, all pet care, [product], [product] and stuff like that, that’s what we do at this site. They also do, um, snack foods and treats, which is like, um, [product], [product], stuff like that, that’s down at [town]. And they also do like the vending machines, they do all that sort of stuff, that’s in [town] but it’s a European – well it’s a worldwide company but we’re mostly European here so a lot of the time you get to go to France and Germany and stuff. I haven’t yet, but other people will because all your teams are across different countries.

Interviewer:	So here do they develop new [products] and then design all the packaging and …?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah. That’s the sort – I mean I’m in Research & Development so we’re just trying to look at what the consumers want and try to make it better from what they want (Yes) That’s basically all I’m doing at the moment.

Interviewer:	OK. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

Subject:	Um, it’s not too bad actually, I mean there’s more men at the top end than there is women, but I don’t – it’s not too bad. There are quite a few powerful women.

Interviewer:	OK. How useful do you think that your degree course has been so far to the work that you’re doing? Have you used any of it?

Subject:	Yeah, I have a bit, but not loads, not as much as I thought, because I’ve been doing a lot of work just with consumers so I’ve been doing a lot of interviews and stuff like that instead, more than I have been doing designing. But now I’m at like the end of a project so I’m – because I’m trying to re-design the [product] pack, so now I’m at the end of it I’m designing, but most of it was just what the consumers want, just to make little changes because they didn’t want a big change to it. But it has been quite handy in like doing things on computers and stuff because I wouldn’t have had a clue otherwise, so that’s been OK.

Interviewer:	Right, OK. Is there anything that you wish you had learned before you started the placement?

Subject:	Um, what do you mean, from my course? (Yeah) Yeah, um. Maybe more general things like essay writing and report writing, because we’ve never done any of that and that was – I’m doing a lot of that now so it’s, I have to keep asking like how they want it doing and stuff because I’m not used to doing any of that, we’re just used to drawing and stuff so it’s not the same. So that would have been useful.

Interviewer:	OK, they’re obviously quite hot on health and safety here. [The researcher had to watch a health and safety video before being allowed on site] Were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

Subject:	Um, yeah, we have the health and safety talks at uni as well when we start in our first year, but that’s it, just like around the workshops and stuff, but nothing [nothing about when you’re going into work] No nothing to prepare you for this.

Interviewer:	Do you think that university could have done more to prepare you for coming on placement?

Subject:	Yeah, a lot more.

Interviewer:	Right, what?

Subject:	Well basically all we got was a talk for about an hour saying, go and find a placement, and then a talk from a woman telling us how to write a CV, and that’s pretty much all we had.

Interviewer:	That was quite late in the year on your course as well wasn’t it?

Subject:	Yeah, and then all we had was – well [company] were the only person who came into our department to do a presentation and that’s when I applied for it. It was, they were the only people who did it early, like most other courses do, because most of my mates didn’t get a placement till like September, so they’re doing a year from September to September and then starting their last year again, so it’s quite late. But they didn’t give us any help in how to write to them or anything and what to do if they offered us a job, because when I got I was just, oh yeah, OK, and I didn’t really find out anything about it or anything like that so, yeah.

Interviewer:	So more advice would have been helpful?

Subject:	Yeah, and more places to look, because I didn’t have a clue where to look, I was just looking on the internet like, design agencies or whatever, and you don’t really know anything about them so it’s, it’d be nicer if they told us where to go or where people have been in the past or whatever.

Interviewer:	OK. Before you started the placement, did the university or your department say what they expected you to gain from going on placement and why placements are a good idea?

Subject:	Well they gave us a booklet of what we should do when we’re on it, but that’s all they gave us really. Because at the beginning of this year we were like, well, what should we be doing, so we like rang up the tutor who deals with it and he was like, it’s all in the booklet, and that’s all he said to us, and we were just like, oh, so we’ve just got this booklet to look through really and we don’t really know what …

Interviewer:	What sort of things were in the booklet?

Subject:	Well it’s just a, um, a dissertation and keep a log of what you’re doing throughout the year, like once a week, writing in what you’re doing, and then a presentation to them at the end of the year, that’s all we know, we don’t really know any details about it or anything, but luckily [company] have got quite a good, um, placement scheme anyway so they kind of guide you on that sort of thing.

Interviewer:	Yeah, I’m going to ask you something about that in a minute.

Subject:	OK.

Interviewer:	How have you found the transition from education to work? Is it easy?

Subject:	Tiring. 

Interviewer:	I was like that when I started (inaudible)

Subject:	It’s different yeah, because we, we can start when we want, so me and [name] – I bring [name] from [university town] as well – so we chose to start at 8, so we have to set off at just gone 7, and that is just hard every morning, and we get back at like 5, but I think that’s the most challenging thing, like the actual work when I’m here is not too bad, it doesn’t go that fast, er, that slowly, but it’s just when I get back I’m just shattered. I love my weekends now. I really treasure my weekends.

Interviewer:	OK. Have you had to face any new issues in work that you hadn’t come across before, like office politics or anything like that?

Subject:	Yeah there’s a lot of office politics. Because I’d, um, I didn’t really realise until I was asked to organise our Christmas party for this year, which was last week, and they were like, right, just go ahead, organise it, this is the budget whatever. So I sent an email round to everyone asking them if they want to go and then got about a million emails back saying, why have you asked this person, and why have you done this, just because there’s so many different little departments and like, they all have their own way of doing things. It’s like, you asked someone from that one and this one, and I was just like, what? And they went, you’ve upset the company politics and I thought, oh my god, it’s a Christmas party for god’s sake, so then I had to like apologise to loads of them. Yeah, it’s just a bit silly I think, but, you get used to it.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. How do you feel about going back to uni when you finish the placement?

Subject:	Scared. Because I’ve seen a lot of my mates, like when I see them out at the weekend and stuff, and they’re saying, oh it’s horrible, like the last year’s just so difficult, so it’s a bit scary because although I’m working like a full day every day here, I’m not doing anything in the evenings and they’re all saying that they’ve been getting up at like 6 every day to do work and working all the way through and I’m just like, oh no. Yeah, it just sounds – I don’t know, I think is it worth it sometimes because, like afterwards I don’t particularly know if I want to be a designer afterwards because it is so much hard work and I just think, oh that last year is just going to be horrendous, and I could just come like into a job like this that’s like, it’s not really really difficult but it’s like quite difficult and you don’t necessarily need a really really good degree in design to do it, so.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that the educational experience reflects what it’s like in industry at all? As in how it’s structured and what you’re taught, or are they two totally different situations?

Subject:	I don’t know, I think they’re quite different. I mean they’ve got the big – here they have like, everybody’s all on one level and you haven’t got a boss, because like everybody sits on one table and stuff and you’re not, like your boss could be sat next to you and even higher people sat next to him and stuff, and you’re all supposed to be just like the same. And that’s a bit weird.

Interviewer:	Does that work in practice?

Subject:	Yeah, I think that’s really weird, because I’m like I’m used to having like a teacher and the head of your department and, I don’t know, you kind of change your behaviour for you’re with don’t you? But these people – like I’m sat next to a student and then my boss is on the next table, and then there’s a person who’s like really high next to him and I’m just, it’s just really weird.

Interviewer:	So is it all open plan offices?

Subject:	Yeah. And I find that really different to anything that I’m used to, because you just have to try …

Interviewer:	That sounds really different to most places I’d say. That’s quite interesting.

Subject:	Yeah, I think that’s what they’re trying to do, but, mm. No-one’s got like their own office or anything, it’s all just one big one.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK, do you think that university and work have like different priorities and goals?

Subject:	Mm, I don’t know, I think they all just want you to get the work done, don’t they, however much they try and say that they’re trying to make you happy at the same time, they really just want to get you to do your work, I don’t know.

Interviewer:	OK, um, do [company] employ many women?

Subject:	Um, yeah, I think – I wouldn’t say it’s even, I mean there’s more men than women, but it’s not, it’s not too bad. It’s a lot more than I thought, like I think there’s 12 students here this year and, um, I think about 8 of them are girls, which I was really shocked by because I thought that – because a lot of them are like quite science-y subjects as well, I just thought there’d have been a lot more boys here than there is girls but yeah, there’s a lot more girls in this one. But I think that’s because they say that they, they like to choose you for the person you are, not the job you’re doing, so if they like you in the interview then they pick you, it’s not necessarily on what qualifications you’ve got and stuff.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK, you were saying earlier about the placement scheme they have in place, how does that work?

Subject:	Um, well before we got here we were sent – well to get, to actually get it we had to fill out a form first, fill out like a – what do you call it? 

Interviewer:	Application form.

Subject:	Yeah, application form first, and then after that we got to an interview, but that was a whole day thing, it wasn’t just an interview. It was like two interviews and, um, we had to do a presentation and then we had to do like a team building thing with the other people at the interview, so it was a whole day thing. So you kind of realised it was quite organised by that. And before we came they sent us loads of stuff to read up on the company and then a booklet of what we could fill in over our first few months just to like, so we had a kind of structure as soon as we got here. And then we have, we have to go through I think it’s about 100 competencies and pick out like 10 that we want to improve on, and 2 that we really want to improve on. We have to keep going through them. We have a personal development portfolio thing that we have to keep adding to what we’re doing, and then we have an appraisal which is about now, I mean mine’s next week, they have it after about six months, to see how we’re going. We have to get feedback from all the people we’ve worked with to see what we can do next year and then we have to set more goals for next year. (OK) So it’s pretty well thought out I think.

Interviewer:	Do you think it’s a good idea doing that then?

Subject:	Yeah, because I think most people in the company do it anyway, so it makes you feel like you’re more …

Interviewer:	A part of it?

Subject:	Yeah, part of it, and you’re not just a student who’s here because like everybody’s doing it and they’re all talking about filling in their PDP or whatever they call it and everybody’s doing the same thing so you feel like you’re more of an employee than just a student here.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Do you think that there’s any way they could improve it at all?

Subject:	Um, I think they do go a bit over the top with the whole competencies thing sometimes. They try and make it out a bit too much, but, you know, they’re American so they do that with a lot of things.

Interviewer:	Yeah. Is your job and what you’re doing what you expected it to be or what you were told to expect before you started?

Subject:	Well no, not really, because when we had the presentation from the people who were here last year, they told us that, to click on the packaging thing when you’re applying and that’s what you’re applying for, so when they ring up saying, you’ve got the job, I just thought that I had the packaging job, I thought that was what it was. Then I found out that a few other people on my course had been, said they’d got a job here as well, so then I rang up and it was Emily who you’re going to interview soon, she got the packaging one, and then we were all in different ones. But they did say at the interview to us, are you interested in any other areas, so I think if you said yes to that then that was when you got shoved in another one, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you get to move round areas?

Subject:	You can go and have like days in other areas but you mainly just stay in yours because you’ve got like your own team and stuff, but I am really enjoying it, it’s not exactly what I thought it’d be but it is quite related so I am enjoying it, but a few other people aren’t.

Interviewer:	OK. You said you were given quite a lot of information about the company when you started. Now that you’ve started, do you think it portrayed an accurate picture of the company?

Subject:	Yeah but I don’t think there was any need for it. It was just all like marketing bumph really, it was all just about the [company] and I didn’t really…

Interviewer:	How great they are?

Subject:	Yeah, just yeah – we’re this good and – because they go by these five principle things like efficiency and all that crap, and it was all just about that, and I’m like, oh my god, what am I going into? But they don’t really mention it much when you’re actually here, it’s not that big a deal, so, it’s not that accurate but…

Interviewer:	OK. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, I’ve been given a project that I’ve just got to do on my own, which I thought was a bit scary at first because they don’t give you any guidance, it’s just, this is what you do, you do it how you want to do it, we’ll meet up in 6 months’ time, so… and I’ve been given quite, I was given quite a big budget for it as well so I got to do some consumer groups and some stuff, so I thought that was quite good because they let me do that all on my own. And um, and then I’m going to be taking over some person’s work who’s leaving because they keep changing the structure of the business so people keep moving around, so everyone’s getting different jobs and I’ll be taking over what some other guy’s doing who’s been here like 30 years, so that’s a bit scary. But yeah, I think it’s good – rather that than not give you enough responsibility I think because it pushes you a bit.

Interviewer:	Yeah. How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

Subject:	Ooh, um….that’s a hard one.

Interviewer:	Good?

Subject:	Yeah, I have really enjoyed it. At the beginning it was a bit slow because the manager wasn’t here for a little while at the beginning so I didn’t really have much to do and I was like, oh I don’t think I’m going to enjoy it, but it’s got a lot better and now, like, I’m a lot more comfortable as well, I’m really enjoying it.

Interviewer:	It just takes a while to like settle in …

Subject:	Yeah, because there are so many different people and stuff that you need to get in contact like with on a daily basis that you need to really know people otherwise you just feel like you’re getting in their way. So it’s good now I’ve been here a while because you can just go and chat to people and I feel like I can do my work a lot easier now. (Yeah, OK) I’m enjoying it, it’s good.

Interviewer:	What do you think are the best and worst things about the placement so far?

Subject:	Um … oh that’s hard. The best was the Christmas party … No I think the best was the project, the big project that I’ve been given to do. I’ve got to hand that in like next week, so that’s been really good because it’s been quite related – it wasn’t given to me by my manager, someone else asked him if I could do it because they thought it was quite related to what I was doing, because it’s packaging. (Yeah) So I think that’s been the best bit because I probably won’t get another one anything like that for the next half of the year. Worst ... I don’t know, it gets a bit boring sometimes. I’m just sat in front of a computer all day every day and it’s up to me to change it really, to go and do something different, and if I’ve got no work that is different then I just have to sit in front of my computer all day and it gets a bit boring because the people around me are a bit old and … old men, not much to talk about, so I think that’s probably the thing that bothers me the most.

Interviewer:	Has the placement met your expectations? Is there anything you thought you would achieve but haven’t yet or anything like that?

Subject:	I think it’s made me a lot more confident, because I have to do like a lot of presentations and stuff. But it’s not as designery as I thought it would be. I don’t think I’m – when I go back I think I’m going to struggle for the first few weeks because I’ve not been doing as much of the stuff that I’ve been doing on my course at all, so… I’ve been trying to do a bit out of the placement because I know that I’m not doing any, or that much of it, so I think, yeah, I was hoping it’d be a bit more related in stuff like drawing and stuff. I’ve not been doing any of that.

Interviewer:	OK. What do you think that you have gained from the placement?

Subject:	Um, a lot of experience. It’s made me a lot more confident with talking to people because I have to talk to that many different high scary people all the time, so that’s made me a lot more confident. I think my presentation skills have got loads better because I’ve had to do – I mean I came to [university] to do the one to the [university] students and I’ve never done anything like that before, and …

Interviewer:	And your course is quite big as well?

Subject:	Yeah, I think there’s about 80 people there, so that was quite scary when they all walked in. But it’s all good because I think we’re going to have to do quite a lot of that in our last year so I think that’ll help.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

Subject:	Um, no not really. I don’t think you can – I think even if it’s not one bit related then it’s still a year in work and it’s still – I mean I think it’s made me a lot more organised, that I have to get up and I have to do stuff and whatever, so I think that’ll help in my last year because I’ll go in and I think I’ll actually get up in the morning and do something rather than, if I haven’t got anything till 12, just stay in bed. I don’t think it can ever be a bad thing because it is just full time work, so it’s not going to …

Interviewer:	You’d recommend it to other people?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, I think you definitely should. I mean it’s going to look really good on anyone’s CV if you’ve done a year work and then gone back to uni.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK, do you think that you’re treated equally to the other placement students?

Subject:	Um, no (laughing) because the ones down in [town] get laptops and I want a laptop. No, I think we’re all treated pretty much the same.

Interviewer:	How many are there here?

Subject:	Here, I think there’s 9 here and 3 up at [site], which is only like a mile away or something, so we sort of say it’s 12 because they all live together in [town], there’s only me and [name] and another girl, [name], who don’t live here. So, yeah, I think we’re all treated pretty much the same. I mean some people aren’t enjoying it as much, I think you may find out in your next interview, [name]’s not having the best time.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think it’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having other placement students here?

Subject:	Advantage, definitely, because when we first got here we were all so scared and it just, it really helped having a lot of other people. We didn’t realise we’d have that many because there wasn’t this many last year, but it really has helped. Because even just like dinner times we all just sit together, we all go to the canteen together.

Interviewer:	So you don’t sit on your own.

Subject:	No, and you don’t have to sit with like your team and be all … yeah, we get to have a laugh more and we all like, if we’re all a bit bored one afternoon we’ll book out a meeting room and pretend to do like some presentations to each other or whatever just for a bit of a break, and they don’t mind, they let us like go off and chat and stuff, so it’s quite good.

Interviewer:	Are you all working in different departments?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah. Well we’re all – I think most of us are in Research & Development but we’re all in different teams within that, so yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you’re treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

Subject:	Most of the time. We’re not allowed in a few, in some meetings and stuff, but apart from that we’re pretty much the same I think.

Interviewer:	You’re not like “the students”?

Subject:	Well yeah we are a bit like that, but I think that’s probably most, that’s our doing really. But yeah, we’re pretty much the same. They do give us the crappy jobs sometimes but it’s not too bad.

Interviewer:	OK, you said you’re in teams – are you actually working in groups and teams all the time?

Subject:	Um, no, I’m mainly on my own because my team’s just pretty much me and my manager, that is it. It was another guy but he’s been moved to a different one now. But some people – I think most people work on their own most of the time but meet up with their team like every day or every few days and show what they’ve done and stuff, and they have like big team meetings all the time. But I’m pretty much on my own most of the time.

Interviewer:	OK, you might not be able to answer any of these questions then, if you’ve not really done much group work. 

Subject:	I have done some, if you want to ask me.

Interviewer:	OK. Are there any particular people that you like or dislike working with? I don’t want you to name names but tell me why you liked or disliked working with particular people.

Subject:	I quite like working with my manager on things because I think he’s a bit, he’s quite on my wavelength. I mean he lets me – he’s quite lenient in that because he knows that I’m quite a designer-y person, he knows that I hate just sitting at a desk all day. So if I want to go and sit and the sofas and do my work, or if I want to work from home some days, he just says I can do it, which is quite cool because he’s sort of the same as me, so he’s like, oh I know, it’s like really restrictive (inaudible). So that’s quite cool, to have someone that’s not just – because a lot of people are fine with just sitting and getting on with it but – so that’s quite good.

Interviewer:	OK. How do you think that doing teamwork at university compares to doing teamwork at work? Is it easier or harder?

Subject:	It’s harder at uni because you can never get people to do stuff. But it’s pretty much the same in that you give each other jobs and then go away and do it and then come back and put everything together what you’ve done, I think that’s pretty similar, sort of thing, yeah.

Interviewer:	Why do you think that people don’t pull their weight as much at uni?

Subject:	Because they can’t be bothered and there’s more important things that they want to do.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been given a mentor in the company?

Subject:	Yes I have.

Interviewer:	How do you feel about that? Do you think it’s good?

Subject:	I think it’s a bit pointless really, because my mentor’s in [town] for half of the week and [town] for the rest of it, so I never – she was here but then she changed jobs and I’ve stayed with her as my mentor, and all we really do is meet up. She says, are you all right, and I go, yeah, and that’s about it. I think it’s a good idea if you do have problems, but I don’t think I’d have any problems with telling my manager if I had something wrong, so that’d be fine with me. But I think it’s good if people don’t feel they can talk to their manager about something and they can have someone who’s more involved with what they’re doing.

Interviewer:	So you treat your manager like a mentor even though he’s not officially?

Subject:	Yeah, I just tell him if I’ve got any troubles, I don’t really go to her. I think they chose her for me because she’s, she was in the packaging team and they thought I was quite interested in that, so, that’s why.

Interviewer:	OK, is there anyone in the company that you regard as a role model?

Subject:	Um.

Interviewer:	There doesn’t have to be.

Subject:	I don’t know. Not really. I like bits of people but I wouldn’t like to be like any particular person.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think makes a good role model then?

Subject:	Oh.

Interviewer:	What are the bits of people that you like?

Subject:	Um. I mean, I like one guy because he’s really really confident and when we first got here he made us feel really like fit in, whereas some people like, people on my table who just sit there and not say anything to you for the first like two months, that doesn’t help. Whereas this guy would always come over and chat to us every day and stuff.

Interviewer:	Made you feel welcome then?

Subject:	Yeah. So I like that about – people who are just normal, not always so business-y. So that’s quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, have you ever had anyone visit you from the university yet?

Subject:	Yeah, our tutor’s been to visit us. We all just came in one room with him and he chatted to us about it. 

Interviewer:	What was the sort of purpose of that visit then?

Subject:	Because he’s supposed to visit us twice a year to see how we’re getting on and if we’ve got any troubles, I think, yeah, but it was a bit pointless really, he didn’t do much, he just came and …

Interviewer:	Did he speak to your manager as well?

Subject:	Yeah, but only because my manager made him. He didn’t speak to anyone else’s, but my manager was like, oh I’d quite like to meet up with him, so I told him and my manager was there. But a few people’s managers weren’t here and one girl he wanted to see – her manager wanted to see him, but he left, so he couldn’t see him.

Interviewer:	OK, did you know the placement tutor well then?

Subject:	Yeah, he was my tutor in my first and second year, so…

Interviewer:	OK, would you be happy to go to him if you did have a problem, or …?

Subject:	No, he’s a weirdo!

Interviewer:	Are you in contact with him at other times or is there anyone else at university that you would get in touch with if you did have problems?

Subject:	Yeah, I’d go to a different person if I, if there was any trouble. I don’t think – well I’d probably go to him but I wouldn’t go to him for like a heart to heart, ever. I would never tell him if I had anything like that. But if it was quite a big thing here then I suppose I’d have to go to him because people would just refer you to him anyway …

Interviewer:	Is he the actual placement tutor?

Subject:	Yeah, I think he goes to everyone, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you know if either the university or here has got like a complaints procedure, if you did any issues?

Subject:	Um, I don’t know, I don’t think so. I think here we just have to go to our mentors and I don’t know what we do at uni if we’ve got any trouble. I think we’re just supposed to go to him.

Interviewer:	OK, I would imagine that you’re all OK on this but we’re interviewing people that are on building sites and stuff, but, are there appropriate facilities for women here?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, there’s really good changing rooms with big mirrors and stuff, it’s like being a star!

Interviewer:	On construction sites and that sometimes they don’t have women’s toilets and things like that.

Subject:	Really?

Interviewer:	Yeah. Are there any occasions when you think that your gender has like determined reactions you’ve got from people?

Subject:	Um, no I don’t think so, no I’ve been pretty OK with that.

Interviewer:	OK, do you still want a career in design technology?

Subject:	Um, I don’t think so. I think – from everything I’ve heard about it it’s just a bit, a bit worrying, because it’s just so, so much hard work for nothing out of it really, and because there’s that many people wanting to do it it’s just really difficult to get a job. I think I’d be more interested in something in like marketing or something like that instead.

Interviewer:	OK. If this company offered you a job when you graduated, would you take it?

Subject:	No, I don’t think so. I mean they do a graduate scheme that, with us being on placement doesn’t get us anything, doesn’t get us onto it any easier or anything, which is a bit, you know, seeing as you’ve already been here for a year, because I think that’s quite an advantage but they don’t, so… But I don’t think I’d apply for it anyway because it’s, it’s um 3 months in each department for a year and it’s moving around different countries, and um, that sounds quite appealing to some people but pet food is not the most interesting thing in the world, so I don’t think that I’d go for it.

Interviewer:	So do you think that your career ambitions have changed from doing the placement or is that how you felt about design before you started?

Subject:	I think I pretty much felt like that about design because that’s why I came to somewhere that wasn’t as designery. I didn’t like apply for any design consultancies or anything because I didn’t think I’d be good enough to do it because it is quite difficult to get one. So I think I felt that before I came here, but I think it’s helped because I’ve seen different areas that I could work in. Like I could work in Research & Development or marketing or stuff like that. You don’t need a specific degree to be able to do it, so I think it has helped to make me a little bit more confident about that because I was worrying a bit about, well what will I do if I don’t do design, there’s nothing. But there is, there’s so many different things.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the placement will still help you when you start work, when you finish uni, even if you don’t go into a related ….?

Subject:	Yeah, I think it will, because I’ve got a lot more broad things out of this than if I’d have just done a design placement. I think I’ve got a lot more …

Interviewer:	Yeah, you mean things like presentation skills and stuff like that?

Subject:	Yeah, I think I’ve got a lot more out of it than I would have done if I’d just done design, so I think it will help.

Interviewer:	OK, I think you said before that you wanted to go travelling when you finish. Do you still want to do that?

Subject:	Yeah. I can’t wait. I’m going to go forever and never come back.

Interviewer:	Are you going to work when you’re travelling?

Subject:	Yeah, hopefully. I mean, yeah, I want to go to places for more than just like a week or a month, I’d like to go to places for quite a while so I’d have to get jobs. I don’t know how I’m going to do that, but we’ll see.

Interviewer:	OK, these are some questions that I asked you in the last interview.

Subject:	I can’t remember what I said.

Interviewer:	It doesn’t matter what you say, it’s just really seeing if it’s easier to answer now that you’ve been in the actual industry for a while.

Subject:	Right, OK.

Interviewer:	So, what five words would you use to describe the design and technology industry?

Subject:	Oh, well this isn’t really designy is it?

Interviewer:	Not what you’re doing, no, but…

Subject:	OK, um – competitive. This is going to take me forever. Um …

Interviewer:	It doesn’t matter if you can’t think of five.

Subject:	Hard working. I don’t know, that’s such a horrible one.

Interviewer:	You’ve said the same things as last time anyway.

Subject:	Have I? Oh great. That’s weird.

Interviewer:	Do you still think that there are advantages and disadvantages to being a woman in quite a male-dominated area?

Subject:	Um, yeah, I don’t think it makes any difference here. I don’t think it’s made any difference in this like half a year that I’ve done so far, but I can see how it could be a disadvantage in some jobs if it’s all male. It’s not too bad here so I don’t think it’s that much of an issue, because there is quite a few women that work here.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think then that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do this sort of work?

Subject:	Yeah, because I think a lot of people shy away from it, from doing – maybe not this one because it’s not too bad here, but design – I mean, I wouldn’t really like to go into a place where it’s just all blokes and I’m the only woman designer. It’d be a bit intimidating.

Interviewer:	Because your course is mainly males isn’t it?

Subject:	Yeah, there’s not many …

Interviewer:	So it’s quite surprising even that – if on the degree courses that there’s more men that it is so sort of even really.

Subject:	Yeah. I don’t mind it at uni – bring it on.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything, thanks very much.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, June, I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Until June next year?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.text: OK, can you tell me a bit about [company] and what they do?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Right, um, we’re not allowed to tell you loads because of our confidentiality thing, but (That’s ok) basically they just do um, all pet care, [product], [product] and stuff like that, that’s what we do at this site. And they also do like the vending machines, they do all that sort of stuff, that’s in [town] but it’s a European – well it’s a worldwide company but we’re mostly European here so a lot of the time you get to go to France and Germany and stuff. turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So here do they develop new [products] and then design all the packaging and …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah. That’s the sort – I mean I’m in Research & Development so we’re just trying to look at what the consumers want and try to make it better from what they want (Yes) That’s basically all I’m doing at the moment.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How would you describe the company’s attitude to women?

turns.speaker: Subject

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How useful do you think that your degree course has been so far to the work that you’re doing? Have you used any of it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I have a bit, but not loads, not as much as I thought, because I’ve been doing a lot of work just with consumers so I’ve been doing a lot of interviews and stuff like that instead, more than I have been doing designing. But now I’m at like the end of a project so I’m – because I’m trying to re-design the [product] pack, so now I’m at the end of it I’m designing, but most of it was just what the consumers want, just to make little changes because they didn’t want a big change to it. But it has been quite handy in like doing things on computers and stuff because I wouldn’t have had a clue otherwise, so that’s been OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, OK. Is there anything that you wish you had learned before you started the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, what do you mean, from my course? (Yeah) Yeah, um. Maybe more general things like essay writing and report writing, because we’ve never done any of that and that was – I’m doing a lot of that now so it’s, I have to keep asking like how they want it doing and stuff because I’m not used to doing any of that, we’re just used to drawing and stuff so it’s not the same. So that would have been useful.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, they’re obviously quite hot on health and safety here. [The researcher had to watch a health and safety video before being allowed on site] Were you taught anything about health and safety at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah, we have the health and safety talks at uni as well when we start in our first year, but that’s it, just like around the workshops and stuff, but nothing [nothing about when you’re going into work] No nothing to prepare you for this.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that university could have done more to prepare you for coming on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, a lot more.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Right, what?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well basically all we got was a talk for about an hour saying, go and find a placement, and then a talk from a woman telling us how to write a CV, and that’s pretty much all we had.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That was quite late in the year on your course as well wasn’t it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and then all we had was – well [company] were the only person who came into our department to do a presentation and that’s when I applied for it. But they didn’t give us any help in how to write to them or anything and what to do if they offered us a job, because when I got I was just, oh yeah, OK, and I didn’t really find out anything about it or anything like that so, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So more advice would have been helpful?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, and more places to look, because I didn’t have a clue where to look, I was just looking on the internet like, design agencies or whatever, and you don’t really know anything about them so it’s, it’d be nicer if they told us where to go or where people have been in the past or whatever.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Before you started the placement, did the university or your department say what they expected you to gain from going on placement and why placements are a good idea?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well they gave us a booklet of what we should do when we’re on it, but that’s all they gave us really. Because at the beginning of this year we were like, well, what should we be doing, so we like rang up the tutor who deals with it and he was like, it’s all in the booklet, and that’s all he said to us, and we were just like, oh, so we’ve just got this booklet to look through really and we don’t really know what …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What sort of things were in the booklet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well it’s just a, um, a dissertation and keep a log of what you’re doing throughout the year, like once a week, writing in what you’re doing, and then a presentation to them at the end of the year, that’s all we know, we don’t really know any details about it or anything, but luckily [company] have got quite a good, um, placement scheme anyway so they kind of guide you on that sort of thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, I’m going to ask you something about that in a minute.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How have you found the transition from education to work? Is it easy?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Tiring.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: I was like that when I started (inaudible)

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s different yeah, because we, we can start when we want, so me and [name] – I bring [name] from [university town] as well – so we chose to start at 8, so we have to set off at just gone 7, and that is just hard every morning, and we get back at like 5, but I think that’s the most challenging thing, like the actual work when I’m here is not too bad, it doesn’t go that fast, er, that slowly, but it’s just when I get back I’m just shattered. I love my weekends now. I really treasure my weekends.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Have you had to face any new issues in work that you hadn’t come across before, like office politics or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah there’s a lot of office politics. Because I’d, um, I didn’t really realise until I was asked to organise our Christmas party for this year, which was last week, and they were like, right, just go ahead, organise it, this is the budget whatever. So I sent an email round to everyone asking them if they want to go and then got about a million emails back saying, why have you asked this person, and why have you done this, just because there’s so many different little departments and like, they all have their own way of doing things. It’s like, you asked someone from that one and this one, and I was just like, what? And they went, you’ve upset the company politics and I thought, oh my god, it’s a Christmas party for god’s sake, so then I had to like apologise to loads of them. Yeah, it’s just a bit silly I think, but, you get used to it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. How do you feel about going back to uni when you finish the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Scared. Because I’ve seen a lot of my mates, like when I see them out at the weekend and stuff, and they’re saying, oh it’s horrible, like the last year’s just so difficult, so it’s a bit scary because although I’m working like a full day every day here, I’m not doing anything in the evenings and they’re all saying that they’ve been getting up at like 6 every day to do work and working all the way through and I’m just like, oh no. Yeah, it just sounds – I don’t know, I think is it worth it sometimes because, like afterwards I don’t particularly know if I want to be a designer afterwards because it is so much hard work and I just think, oh that last year is just going to be horrendous, and I could just come like into a job like this that’s like, it’s not really really difficult but it’s like quite difficult and you don’t necessarily need a really really good degree in design to do it, so.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that the educational experience reflects what it’s like in industry at all? As in how it’s structured and what you’re taught, or are they two totally different situations?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know, I think they’re quite different. And that’s a bit weird.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Does that work in practice?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think that’s really weird, because I’m like I’m used to having like a teacher and the head of your department and, I don’t know, you kind of change your behaviour for you’re with don’t you? But these people – like I’m sat next to a student and then my boss is on the next table, and then there’s a person who’s like really high next to him and I’m just, it’s just really weird.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So is it all open plan offices?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. And I find that really different to anything that I’m used to, because you just have to try …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That sounds really different to most places I’d say. That’s quite interesting.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think that’s what they’re trying to do, but, mm. No-one’s got like their own office or anything, it’s all just one big one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, do you think that university and work have like different priorities and goals?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, I don’t know, I think they all just want you to get the work done, don’t they, however much they try and say that they’re trying to make you happy at the same time, they really just want to get you to do your work, I don’t know.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, um, do [company] employ many women?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah, I think – I wouldn’t say it’s even, I mean there’s more men than women, but it’s not, it’s not too bad. It’s a lot more than I thought, like I think there’s 12 students here this year and, um, I think about 8 of them are girls, which I was really shocked by because I thought that – because a lot of them are like quite science-y subjects as well, I just thought there’d have been a lot more boys here than there is girls but yeah, there’s a lot more girls in this one. But I think that’s because they say that they, they like to choose you for the person you are, not the job you’re doing, so if they like you in the interview then they pick you, it’s not necessarily on what qualifications you’ve got and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, you were saying earlier about the placement scheme they have in place, how does that work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, well before we got here we were sent – well to get, to actually get it we had to fill out a form first, fill out like a – what do you call it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Application form.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, application form first, and then after that we got to an interview, but that was a whole day thing, it wasn’t just an interview. It was like two interviews and, um, we had to do a presentation and then we had to do like a team building thing with the other people at the interview, so it was a whole day thing. So you kind of realised it was quite organised by that. And before we came they sent us loads of stuff to read up on the company and then a booklet of what we could fill in over our first few months just to like, so we had a kind of structure as soon as we got here. And then we have, we have to go through I think it’s about 100 competencies and pick out like 10 that we want to improve on, and 2 that we really want to improve on. We have to keep going through them. We have a personal development portfolio thing that we have to keep adding to what we’re doing, and then we have an appraisal which is about now, I mean mine’s next week, they have it after about six months, to see how we’re going. We have to get feedback from all the people we’ve worked with to see what we can do next year and then we have to set more goals for next year. (OK) So it’s pretty well thought out I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it’s a good idea doing that then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because I think most people in the company do it anyway, so it makes you feel like you’re more …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: A part of it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, part of it, and you’re not just a student who’s here because like everybody’s doing it and they’re all talking about filling in their PDP or whatever they call it and everybody’s doing the same thing so you feel like you’re more of an employee than just a student here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Do you think that there’s any way they could improve it at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I think they do go a bit over the top with the whole competencies thing sometimes. They try and make it out a bit too much, but, you know, they’re American so they do that with a lot of things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Is your job and what you’re doing what you expected it to be or what you were told to expect before you started?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well no, not really, because when we had the presentation from the people who were here last year, they told us that, to click on the packaging thing when you’re applying and that’s what you’re applying for, so when they ring up saying, you’ve got the job, I just thought that I had the packaging job, I thought that was what it was. Then I found out that a few other people on my course had been, said they’d got a job here as well, so then I rang up and it was Emily who you’re going to interview soon, she got the packaging one, and then we were all in different ones. But they did say at the interview to us, are you interested in any other areas, so I think if you said yes to that then that was when you got shoved in another one, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you get to move round areas?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: You can go and have like days in other areas but you mainly just stay in yours because you’ve got like your own team and stuff, but I am really enjoying it, it’s not exactly what I thought it’d be but it is quite related so I am enjoying it, but a few other people aren’t.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. You said you were given quite a lot of information about the company when you started. Now that you’ve started, do you think it portrayed an accurate picture of the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah but I don’t think there was any need for it. It was just all like marketing bumph really, it was all just about the [company] and I didn’t really…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How great they are?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, just yeah – we’re this good and – because they go by these five principle things like efficiency and all that crap, and it was all just about that, and I’m like, oh my god, what am I going into? But they don’t really mention it much when you’re actually here, it’s not that big a deal, so, it’s not that accurate but…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you feel like you’ve been given an appropriate level of responsibility?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, I’ve been given a project that I’ve just got to do on my own, which I thought was a bit scary at first because they don’t give you any guidance, it’s just, this is what you do, you do it how you want to do it, we’ll meet up in 6 months’ time, so… and I’ve been given quite, I was given quite a big budget for it as well so I got to do some consumer groups and some stuff, so I thought that was quite good because they let me do that all on my own. And um, and then I’m going to be taking over some person’s work who’s leaving because they keep changing the structure of the business so people keep moving around, so everyone’s getting different jobs and I’ll be taking over what some other guy’s doing who’s been here like 30 years, so that’s a bit scary. But yeah, I think it’s good – rather that than not give you enough responsibility I think because it pushes you a bit.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. How would you summarise your placement experience so far then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Ooh, um….that’s a hard one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Good?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I have really enjoyed it. At the beginning it was a bit slow because the manager wasn’t here for a little while at the beginning so I didn’t really have much to do and I was like, oh I don’t think I’m going to enjoy it, but it’s got a lot better and now, like, I’m a lot more comfortable as well, I’m really enjoying it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It just takes a while to like settle in …

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because there are so many different people and stuff that you need to get in contact like with on a daily basis that you need to really know people otherwise you just feel like you’re getting in their way. So it’s good now I’ve been here a while because you can just go and chat to people and I feel like I can do my work a lot easier now. (Yeah, OK) I’m enjoying it, it’s good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think are the best and worst things about the placement so far?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um … oh that’s hard. The best was the Christmas party … No I think the best was the project, the big project that I’ve been given to do. I’ve got to hand that in like next week, so that’s been really good because it’s been quite related – it wasn’t given to me by my manager, someone else asked him if I could do it because they thought it was quite related to what I was doing, because it’s packaging. (Yeah) So I think that’s been the best bit because I probably won’t get another one anything like that for the next half of the year. Worst ... I don’t know, it gets a bit boring sometimes. I’m just sat in front of a computer all day every day and it’s up to me to change it really, to go and do something different, and if I’ve got no work that is different then I just have to sit in front of my computer all day and it gets a bit boring because the people around me are a bit old and … old men, not much to talk about, so I think that’s probably the thing that bothers me the most.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has the placement met your expectations? Is there anything you thought you would achieve but haven’t yet or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s made me a lot more confident, because I have to do like a lot of presentations and stuff. But it’s not as designery as I thought it would be. I don’t think I’m – when I go back I think I’m going to struggle for the first few weeks because I’ve not been doing as much of the stuff that I’ve been doing on my course at all, so… I’ve been trying to do a bit out of the placement because I know that I’m not doing any, or that much of it, so I think, yeah, I was hoping it’d be a bit more related in stuff like drawing and stuff. I’ve not been doing any of that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. What do you think that you have gained from the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, a lot of experience. It’s made me a lot more confident with talking to people because I have to talk to that many different high scary people all the time, so that’s made me a lot more confident. I think my presentation skills have got loads better because I’ve had to do – I mean I came to [university] to do the one to the [university] students and I’ve never done anything like that before, and …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: And your course is quite big as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think there’s about 80 people there, so that was quite scary when they all walked in. But it’s all good because I think we’re going to have to do quite a lot of that in our last year so I think that’ll help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that there are any drawbacks to doing a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no not really. I don’t think you can – I think even if it’s not one bit related then it’s still a year in work and it’s still – I mean I think it’s made me a lot more organised, that I have to get up and I have to do stuff and whatever, so I think that’ll help in my last year because I’ll go in and I think I’ll actually get up in the morning and do something rather than, if I haven’t got anything till 12, just stay in bed. I don’t think it can ever be a bad thing because it is just full time work, so it’s not going to …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’d recommend it to other people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, I think you definitely should. I mean it’s going to look really good on anyone’s CV if you’ve done a year work and then gone back to uni.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK, do you think that you’re treated equally to the other placement students?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no (laughing) because the ones down in [town] get laptops and I want a laptop. No, I think we’re all treated pretty much the same.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How many are there here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Here, I think there’s 9 here and 3 up at [site], which is only like a mile away or something, so we sort of say it’s 12 because they all live together in [town], there’s only me and [name] and another girl, [name], who don’t live here. So, yeah, I think we’re all treated pretty much the same. I mean some people aren’t enjoying it as much, I think you may find out in your next interview, [name]’s not having the best time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think it’s been an advantage or a disadvantage having other placement students here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Advantage, definitely, because when we first got here we were all so scared and it just, it really helped having a lot of other people. We didn’t realise we’d have that many because there wasn’t this many last year, but it really has helped. Because even just like dinner times we all just sit together, we all go to the canteen together.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you don’t sit on your own.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, and you don’t have to sit with like your team and be all … yeah, we get to have a laugh more and we all like, if we’re all a bit bored one afternoon we’ll book out a meeting room and pretend to do like some presentations to each other or whatever just for a bit of a break, and they don’t mind, they let us like go off and chat and stuff, so it’s quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you all working in different departments?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah. Well we’re all – I think most of us are in Research & Development but we’re all in different teams within that, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you’re treated the same as the permanent members of staff?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Most of the time. We’re not allowed in a few, in some meetings and stuff, but apart from that we’re pretty much the same I think.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’re not like “the students”?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well yeah we are a bit like that, but I think that’s probably most, that’s our doing really. But yeah, we’re pretty much the same. They do give us the crappy jobs sometimes but it’s not too bad.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you said you’re in teams – are you actually working in groups and teams all the time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no, I’m mainly on my own because my team’s just pretty much me and my manager, that is it. It was another guy but he’s been moved to a different one now. But some people – I think most people work on their own most of the time but meet up with their team like every day or every few days and show what they’ve done and stuff, and they have like big team meetings all the time. But I’m pretty much on my own most of the time.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, you might not be able to answer any of these questions then, if you’ve not really done much group work.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I have done some, if you want to ask me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are there any particular people that you like or dislike working with? I don’t want you to name names but tell me why you liked or disliked working with particular people.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I quite like working with my manager on things because I think he’s a bit, he’s quite on my wavelength. I mean he lets me – he’s quite lenient in that because he knows that I’m quite a designer-y person, he knows that I hate just sitting at a desk all day. So if I want to go and sit and the sofas and do my work, or if I want to work from home some days, he just says I can do it, which is quite cool because he’s sort of the same as me, so he’s like, oh I know, it’s like really restrictive (inaudible). So that’s quite cool, to have someone that’s not just – because a lot of people are fine with just sitting and getting on with it but – so that’s quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. How do you think that doing teamwork at university compares to doing teamwork at work? Is it easier or harder?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: It’s harder at uni because you can never get people to do stuff. But it’s pretty much the same in that you give each other jobs and then go away and do it and then come back and put everything together what you’ve done, I think that’s pretty similar, sort of thing, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Why do you think that people don’t pull their weight as much at uni?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because they can’t be bothered and there’s more important things that they want to do.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been given a mentor in the company?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yes I have.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: How do you feel about that? Do you think it’s good?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s a bit pointless really, because my mentor’s in [town] for half of the week and [town] for the rest of it, so I never – she was here but then she changed jobs and I’ve stayed with her as my mentor, and all we really do is meet up. She says, are you all right, and I go, yeah, and that’s about it. I think it’s a good idea if you do have problems, but I don’t think I’d have any problems with telling my manager if I had something wrong, so that’d be fine with me. But I think it’s good if people don’t feel they can talk to their manager about something and they can have someone who’s more involved with what they’re doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So you treat your manager like a mentor even though he’s not officially?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I just tell him if I’ve got any troubles, I don’t really go to her. I think they chose her for me because she’s, she was in the packaging team and they thought I was quite interested in that, so, that’s why.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, is there anyone in the company that you regard as a role model?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: There doesn’t have to be.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t know. Not really. I like bits of people but I wouldn’t like to be like any particular person.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think makes a good role model then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What are the bits of people that you like?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um. I mean, I like one guy because he’s really really confident and when we first got here he made us feel really like fit in, whereas some people like, people on my table who just sit there and not say anything to you for the first like two months, that doesn’t help. Whereas this guy would always come over and chat to us every day and stuff.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Made you feel welcome then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. So I like that about – people who are just normal, not always so business-y. So that’s quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you ever had anyone visit you from the university yet?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, our tutor’s been to visit us. We all just came in one room with him and he chatted to us about it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What was the sort of purpose of that visit then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Because he’s supposed to visit us twice a year to see how we’re getting on and if we’ve got any troubles, I think, yeah, but it was a bit pointless really, he didn’t do much, he just came and …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did he speak to your manager as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, but only because my manager made him. He didn’t speak to anyone else’s, but my manager was like, oh I’d quite like to meet up with him, so I told him and my manager was there. But a few people’s managers weren’t here and one girl he wanted to see – her manager wanted to see him, but he left, so he couldn’t see him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you know the placement tutor well then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, he was my tutor in my first and second year, so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you be happy to go to him if you did have a problem, or …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, he’s a weirdo!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you in contact with him at other times or is there anyone else at university that you would get in touch with if you did have problems?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’d go to a different person if I, if there was any trouble. I don’t think – well I’d probably go to him but I wouldn’t go to him for like a heart to heart, ever. I would never tell him if I had anything like that. But if it was quite a big thing here then I suppose I’d have to go to him because people would just refer you to him anyway …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is he the actual placement tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think he goes to everyone, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you know if either the university or here has got like a complaints procedure, if you did any issues?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t know, I don’t think so. I think here we just have to go to our mentors and I don’t know what we do at uni if we’ve got any trouble. I think we’re just supposed to go to him.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I would imagine that you’re all OK on this but we’re interviewing people that are on building sites and stuff, but, are there appropriate facilities for women here?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah, there’s really good changing rooms with big mirrors and stuff, it’s like being a star!

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: On construction sites and that sometimes they don’t have women’s toilets and things like that.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah. Are there any occasions when you think that your gender has like determined reactions you’ve got from people?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, no I don’t think so, no I’ve been pretty OK with that.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you still want a career in design technology?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, I don’t think so. I think – from everything I’ve heard about it it’s just a bit, a bit worrying, because it’s just so, so much hard work for nothing out of it really, and because there’s that many people wanting to do it it’s just really difficult to get a job. I think I’d be more interested in something in like marketing or something like that instead.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. If this company offered you a job when you graduated, would you take it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, I don’t think so. I mean they do a graduate scheme that, with us being on placement doesn’t get us anything, doesn’t get us onto it any easier or anything, which is a bit, you know, seeing as you’ve already been here for a year, because I think that’s quite an advantage but they don’t, so… But I don’t think I’d apply for it anyway because it’s, it’s um 3 months in each department for a year and it’s moving around different countries, and um, that sounds quite appealing to some people but pet food is not the most interesting thing in the world, so I don’t think that I’d go for it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So do you think that your career ambitions have changed from doing the placement or is that how you felt about design before you started?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think I pretty much felt like that about design because that’s why I came to somewhere that wasn’t as designery. I didn’t like apply for any design consultancies or anything because I didn’t think I’d be good enough to do it because it is quite difficult to get one. So I think I felt that before I came here, but I think it’s helped because I’ve seen different areas that I could work in. Like I could work in Research & Development or marketing or stuff like that. You don’t need a specific degree to be able to do it, so I think it has helped to make me a little bit more confident about that because I was worrying a bit about, well what will I do if I don’t do design, there’s nothing. But there is, there’s so many different things.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the placement will still help you when you start work, when you finish uni, even if you don’t go into a related ….?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think it will, because I’ve got a lot more broad things out of this than if I’d have just done a design placement. I think I’ve got a lot more …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, you mean things like presentation skills and stuff like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think I’ve got a lot more out of it than I would have done if I’d just done design, so I think it will help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, I think you said before that you wanted to go travelling when you finish. Do you still want to do that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I can’t wait. I’m going to go forever and never come back.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Are you going to work when you’re travelling?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, hopefully. I mean, yeah, I want to go to places for more than just like a week or a month, I’d like to go to places for quite a while so I’d have to get jobs. I don’t know how I’m going to do that, but we’ll see.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, these are some questions that I asked you in the last interview.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I can’t remember what I said.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It doesn’t matter what you say, it’s just really seeing if it’s easier to answer now that you’ve been in the actual industry for a while.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Right, OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So, what five words would you use to describe the design and technology industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Oh, well this isn’t really designy is it?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Not what you’re doing, no, but…

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: OK, um – competitive. This is going to take me forever. Um …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: It doesn’t matter if you can’t think of five.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hard working. I don’t know, that’s such a horrible one.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’ve said the same things as last time anyway.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Have I? Oh great. That’s weird.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you still think that there are advantages and disadvantages to being a woman in quite a male-dominated area?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Um, yeah, I don’t think it makes any difference here. I don’t think it’s made any difference in this like half a year that I’ve done so far, but I can see how it could be a disadvantage in some jobs if it’s all male. It’s not too bad here so I don’t think it’s that much of an issue, because there is quite a few women that work here.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think then that more women should be encouraged or enabled to do this sort of work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, because I think a lot of people shy away from it, from doing – maybe not this one because it’s not too bad here, but design – I mean, I wouldn’t really like to go into a place where it’s just all blokes and I’m the only woman designer. It’d be a bit intimidating.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Because your course is mainly males isn’t it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, there’s not many …

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So it’s quite surprising even that – if on the degree courses that there’s more men that it is so sort of even really.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. I don’t mind it at uni – bring it on.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s everything, thanks very much.
